491.title: Don't lean on mortals
491.hook: don't rest your hopes on people who cannot save you (Sukhmani 14)
491.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the fourteenth ashtpadi's first stanza on the vain reliance on mortals, while Sikh life continues to rest heavily on sangat, family and community service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 14, siaanap, and your line: drop the cleverness. Did you put down one plan you'd been circling? The salok said keep one hope. Today the first stanza asks where that hope should rest. Day four hundred ninety-one.

A friend said he'd put in a word for you. He knows the manager. It's basically done, he said. So you stopped applying anywhere else. Two weeks, three weeks. Then a text: so sorry, it didn't work out, they went internal. He meant well. He just couldn't carry what you'd put on him. It's easy to lean your whole weight on somebody like that, a friend, a boss, a parent, a partner, and feel the floor tilt when they can't hold it. Today the fourteenth ashtpadi talks about where to put your weight.
screen: `HE'LL PUT IN A WORD FOR YOU.` → `YOU STOP LOOKING ANYWHERE ELSE.` → `THE FLOOR TILTS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: know that all reliance on mortals is in vain; the Giver is the One Lord alone. The key word is tek. A tek is a prop, a support, the thing you lean on, like a walking stick or a post you rest your back against. Brithee means useless, in vain. So: the human prop won't bear the weight. Now, this could sound bleak, even cold. Don't trust people? But that's not what Sikh life looks like at all. The whole tradition runs on people: the sangat, the company; the langar, cooked and served by volunteers; families who carry each other for generations. Sukhmani itself, a few days back, told us to take shelter in the company of the good. So the stanza can't mean, have nothing to do with people. It's narrower and kinder than that. It's about the last weight. The final hope. The thing you'd collapse without. People are limited, not because they're bad, but because they're people. They get sick, they forget, they move away, they die. Your friend with the manager couldn't control the manager. When the whole of your hope rests on one person, you've asked them to be something no human can be. And when they fail, you end up resenting them for being human. Lean your final weight on the One, the stanza says, and something surprising happens to your relationships. You can love people without crushing them. Your friend can be just a friend: a good one, a limited one, and that's enough. Tomorrow the stanza goes on to the Giver. Today, just notice where your weight is.
screen: `TEK: THE PROP YOU LEAN ON.` · `NOT: HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH PEOPLE.` · `PEOPLE ARE LIMITED, NOT BAD.` · `LOVE WITHOUT CRUSHING.` · then, large: `LEAN ON THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel where your weight rests. Sit back and let your body lean into the chair, or the wall, or the floor. Notice what's holding you right now. Then bring to mind one person you've been leaning on very hard lately, maybe without realizing it. See them kindly: a person, with limits. Gently take a little of the weight off them, and let it rest deeper, wherever you sense something steadier than any one person. If you pray, rest it in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Tek, a prop, a support. Maanukh kee tek, the human prop, can't bear your final weight; Sukhmani says rest that weight in the One.
Your line: lean on the one. Today, when someone lets you down a little, forgive them for being human, and move your hope one step deeper. Day four hundred ninety-one.

492.title: The one Giver
492.hook: the Giver alone gives; all others are passing (Sukhmani 14)
492.howItsDone: Sikhs call God daataa, the Giver, in daily speech and in Gurbani; Japji Sahib asks never to forget the one Giver of all beings, and Sukhmani's fourteenth ashtpadi names the Giver whose gift satisfies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tek, and your line: lean on the one. Did you forgive someone for being human? Today the same stanza names the One you lean on: the Giver. Day four hundred ninety-two.

Pick up whatever you ate last. A piece of toast, say. Who gave you that? The store, sure. But the store got it from a bakery, the bakery from a mill, the mill from a farm. The farmer planted, but didn't make the seed grow, or the rain fall, or the sun rise. Follow any gift back far enough and the chain of hands gets very long, and then it runs out of hands. Sukhmani has a name for what's at the end of the chain. Today: the one Giver.
screen: `WHO GAVE YOU THE TOAST?` → `STORE, BAKERY, MILL, FARM.` → `THE CHAIN RUNS OUT OF HANDS.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth ashtpadi's first stanza, which yesterday warned against leaning on mortals, goes on in paraphrase: the Giver is the One Lord alone. By whose gift a person is satisfied, and thirst does not come back to cling to them. Look at that second half, because it's the real point. There are two kinds of giving in this stanza. One kind fills you for a moment and leaves you hungrier: the raise that makes you want a bigger raise, the praise that makes you need more praise. The other kind leaves you satisfied, aghaai, full, with the thirst gone. Sukhmani says only the One gives the second kind. The Giver has come up much earlier on this path. In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak asks the Guru for one understanding, and it's this: there is one Giver of all beings; may I never forget Him. Daataa, in Punjabi. The Giver. It's an everyday name for God in Sikh speech. People can thank the Giver in passing, in a word or two, when the crops come in, when the baby is born, when the test results are good. Now notice what that does to every other gift. Your boss, your parents, the farmer, the stranger who held the door: they're real, and they deserve real thanks. But in this picture they're hands in the chain, not the source. Their gifts pass through them. That's not an insult to them. It's a relief. Nobody has to be the bottom of your well. And everything given to you, from the toast to the breath you just took, is a thread you can follow back to the same place.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF GIVING.` · `AGHAAI: FULL, AND THE THIRST GONE.` · `DAATAA: THE GIVER, IN JAPJI.` · `EVERY HAND A LINK IN THE CHAIN.` · then, large: `ONE GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow one gift back. Choose one thing you have right now: the water you drank, the clothes you're wearing, the breath in your chest. Trace it back, hand by hand, as far as you can. Thank each hand quietly as you pass it. When you run out of hands, stop, and rest there a moment. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver in whatever words are yours. The bell holds the time.
Daataa, the Giver. Whose gift leaves you full, with the thirst gone; every other giver is a hand in the chain.
Your line: one giver. Today, when you thank someone, thank them fully, and then let the thanks travel one step further back. Day four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: Living ashtpadi 14
493.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, earning by honest work, one of the core Sikh duties along with remembering the Name and sharing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daataa, and your line: one giver. Did a thank-you travel one step further back? Today we close the fourteenth ashtpadi with a story from the janamsakhis. Day four hundred ninety-three.

Two invitations arrive in the same town on the same day. One is from a rich official, Malik Bhago, who is throwing a grand feast and expects every holy man around to attend. The other is from Bhai Lalo, a carpenter, who can offer only plain, coarse bread. Guru Nanak is in town. Everyone assumes he'll go to the feast. He goes to the carpenter's house. And when the official, insulted, demands to know why, the answer, as Sikhs tell it, is a moment from the janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life.
screen: `TWO INVITATIONS, ONE TOWN.` → `A FEAST, OR A CARPENTER'S BREAD.` → `HE GOES TO THE CARPENTER.`

segments.voice: Here's how the story goes. Guru Nanak takes Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a rich cake from Malik Bhago's feast in the other, and squeezes both. From Lalo's bread, the story says, comes milk. From Bhago's, blood. Bhago's wealth had been squeezed out of the poor; Lalo's bread had been earned with his own hands. It's a story, told and retold, not a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs hear it as a picture rather than a lab report. But the picture is about exactly what the fourteenth ashtpadi has been saying. Malik Bhago is siaanap made flesh: the clever official, working angles, rich from other people's labor, leaning on power and on people who could be bought. Lalo is the opposite. Simple, straight, one hope. Sikhs have a word for Lalo's kind of living: kirat. Honest work. Kirat karni, earning by honest labor, is one of three duties Sikh teaching names together, alongside remembering the Name and sharing what you have. It isn't glamorous. It's showing up, doing the job straight, charging a fair price, not cutting the corner when nobody would notice. And notice what simplicity buys you. Malik Bhago has to keep track of his schemes, his debts, his flatterers. Lalo has nothing to keep track of. His bread is just bread. That's living ashtpadi 14: not becoming naive, but choosing, again and again, the way that needs no angles.
screen: `MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.` · `A STORY, HEARD AS A PICTURE.` · `KIRAT: HONEST WORK.` · `NOTHING TO KEEP TRACK OF.` · then, large: `SIMPLE, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the straight way through one thing. Think of something on your plate this week where there's a shortcut, a little angle, a convenient half-truth. Picture the angled way, and feel how much tracking it would take. Then picture the plain way: the honest email, the fair price, the work done properly. Feel how much lighter it is to carry. Choose it, here, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Kirat, honest work. Bhai Lalo's plain bread, the simple straight way that needs no angles and leaves nothing to keep track of.
Your line: simple, straight. Once today, choose the straightforward way over the clever one, even if the clever one would save a little time. Day four hundred ninety-three.

494.title: Ashtpadi 15, salok: all powers
494.hook: sarab kalaa bharpoor: He is full of every power (Sukhmani 15)
494.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fifteenth ashtpadi with the salok sarab kalaa bharpoor, and in daily life chardi kalaa, rising spirits, is an answer Sikhs give to 'how are you?', in good times and hard ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 14, kirat, and your line: simple, straight. Did you pick the straight way over the clever one? Today, ashtpadi fifteen opens with a word you may already know from a Sikh greeting. Day four hundred ninety-four.

Ask a Sikh how they're doing and you might hear two words: chardi kalaa. It can be said after good news, and after bad. A flooded basement, a hard diagnosis, a job lost, and still: chardi kalaa. Rising spirits. Ever-ascending energy. It's a deeply Sikh phrase, and it can sound almost stubborn, cheerful in the face of everything. But where does that rising energy come from? The answer is hiding in the second word, kalaa. And today, the salok of the fifteenth ashtpadi puts that same word right at its center.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU? CHARDI KALAA.` → `AFTER GOOD NEWS, AND AFTER BAD.` → `WHERE DOES THE RISING COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: God is brimful of every power, the knower of every pain. By remembering Him we are carried across; Nanak is a sacrifice to Him. Three words to open. Sarab: all, every. Bharpoor: brimful, full to the edge, like a bucket that can't take one more drop. And kalaa. Kalaa is a rich word. It can mean power, but also skill, art, a craft, and in older Indian usage, a phase of the moon, one sliver of its light. So sarab kalaa bharpoor is something like: full to the brim with every power, every art, every light there is. In the salok's picture, there is no power anywhere that isn't already full in the One. Now come back to chardi kalaa. Read beside this salok, chardi kalaa, rising power, isn't a boast of home-made strength. It points the other way: the power rising in a person comes from the One who is full of all of it. Spirits can rise after a flood because, in this picture, the source isn't the basement. That's also why the salok's second half matters. The One full of every power is also birthaa jaananhaar, the knower of every pain. All that power isn't cold or far away. It knows what's hurting. Tomorrow we stay with that half of the line. Today, one picture to sit with: next to sarab kalaa bharpoor, every person is small. The salok doesn't make that frightening. Being small beside the One full of every power, who also knows every pain, is pictured as being held.
screen: `SARAB: ALL. BHARPOOR: BRIMFUL.` · `KALAA: POWER, ART, A SLIVER OF MOON.` · `CHARDI KALAA: RISING, NOT SELF-MADE.` · `SMALL, AND HELD.` · then, large: `HE HOLDS ALL POWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel small, safely. If you can see the sky, look at it; if not, picture the night sky, all of it, star past star. Let yourself be the size you actually are. Notice if there's any fear in that. Then try holding the salok's picture instead: everything out there brimful of one power, and that power knowing you. Small, and held. Let your breathing slow into it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly. The bell holds the time.
Kalaa, power, skill, art. Sarab kalaa bharpoor, brimful of every power, and the knower of every pain. The same kalaa rises in chardi kalaa.
Your line: he holds all power. Today, when something feels too big, name it plainly, and set the salok's words beside it: brimful of every power. Day four hundred ninety-four.

495.title: He knows your pain
495.hook: the Lord knows every heart's pain (Sukhmani 15)
495.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib name God birthaa jaananhaar, the knower of every pain, in the fifteenth ashtpadi's salok, and many bring their troubles silently to the Guru in prayer and in the Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 15, kalaa, and your line: he holds all power. Did something too big for you feel a little lighter? Today, the other half of that same salok. Day four hundred ninety-five.

The doctor asks you to rate your pain from one to ten, and you freeze. Is it a six? A seven? It doesn't feel like a number. It feels like a color, or a weight, or a sound that won't stop. Some pain can't be explained to anybody. You try, and the words come out too small, or too dramatic, and the person nods kindly and clearly doesn't get it. Today the fifteenth ashtpadi names the One who doesn't need the number.
screen: `RATE YOUR PAIN, ONE TO TEN.` → `IT DOESN'T FEEL LIKE A NUMBER.` → `NO NUMBER NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok called God sarab kalaa bharpoor, brimful of every power. In the same breath it says birthaa jaananhaar. Jaananhaar: the one who knows. Birthaa: the inner condition, especially the pain of it, what's going on in you that nobody can see. So: the knower of every heart's pain. Put the two halves together and they say something that matters a great deal. Power without knowing would be frightening, a force that can do anything but doesn't notice you. Knowing without power would be sad, a friend who understands but can't help. The salok holds both in one line: the One who can do anything already knows exactly what's wrong. The first stanza of the ashtpadi gives the picture a tender name. It calls God the mender of the broken: the one who joins what has snapped, like a carpenter fitting a cracked chair leg back together. The same stanza says God carries the care of all beings in mind. Notice what this doesn't say. It doesn't say the pain isn't real, or that it's deserved, or that it'll be gone by tomorrow. Gurbani is honest about suffering; the Gurus lived through plenty of it, and Guru Arjan himself, who wrote these words, was later tortured and killed. What it says is that the pain is known. You don't have to find the right number. You don't have to explain it well. The knowing is already there. For many Sikhs, that's where prayer starts: not with getting the words right, but with remembering that the hurt is already known.
screen: `BIRTHAA: THE PAIN INSIDE.` · `POWER AND KNOWING, ONE LINE.` · `THE MENDER OF THE BROKEN.` · `NO NEED TO EXPLAIN IT WELL.` · then, large: `HE KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one pain, silently. Let one hurt come to mind, big or small: a worry, an ache, a grief that won't settle. Don't explain it. Don't rate it. Just turn toward it and let it be seen, the way you'd hold a cut finger up to someone who loves you. If you pray, you can offer it to Waheguru without words. If you don't, simply let it be fully known by you, for once, without hurrying away. The bell holds the time.
Birthaa, the heart's inner pain. The One full of every power also knows it, the mender of what's broken.
Your line: he knows. Today, when someone you know seems to be hurting, don't ask them to explain. Just let them know you see it. Day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Nothing on our own
496.hook: on our own we can do nothing; all happens in His color (Sukhmani 15)
496.howItsDone: Gurbani often speaks of being dyed in the Name, like cloth in fast madder dye, and Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's fifteenth ashtpadi hear that nothing is done by one's own doing alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birthaa, and your line: he knows. Did you let someone know you saw what they were carrying? Today the fifteenth ashtpadi turns to everything we do, and gives it a color. Day four hundred ninety-six.

In old Punjab, cloth was dyed by hand. You'd soak plain white cotton in a vat, and when you lifted it out, it had become saffron, or indigo, or deep red. Here's the thing about a good dye: it doesn't sit on top of the cloth like paint. It goes into every thread. You can't scrape it off. The cloth is still cloth, but now every part of it carries the color. Gurbani returns to that picture. Today it's the way into a hard teaching: nothing on our own.
screen: `WHITE COTTON IN A VAT.` → `SAFFRON, INDIGO, DEEP RED.` → `THE COLOR GOES INTO EVERY THREAD.`

segments.voice: Back in the eleventh ashtpadi, Sukhmani called God the doer of all. The fifteenth comes back to that thought from a different side. Its first stanza says, in paraphrase: nothing happens by a person's own doing, though they long for it a hundred times. Gurbani elsewhere gives that thought a color. Rang means color, and dye. But in Punjabi it also means joy, love, mood, the delight of a festival. So when Gurbani speaks of being dyed in His rang, it's saying more than: God controls everything. It pictures everything soaked in God, the way dyed cloth is soaked in color. Our actions are still ours, the way the cloth is still cloth. Sikhs work hard, study, serve, and plan; nobody is told to sit and wait. But in this picture every thread of that doing is already colored by the One Sukhmani calls the Giver, the One full of every power. The strength in the arms, the idea that arrived, the breath that let the sentence finish: none of it, the stanza says, comes by our own doing alone. One version of this picture in Gurbani is a deep red dye from the madder root, majeeth. Cloth dyed with majeeth was said to keep its color through every wash. Hymns ask to be dyed like that, so deeply in the Name that nothing washes it out. So nothing on our own isn't an insult to your effort. It's a description of what your effort is made of. And it leads straight to the practice: when the doing is soaked in someone else's color, the natural response, when it's done, is thanks.
screen: `THE DOER OF ALL, ANOTHER SIDE.` · `RANG: COLOR, DYE, JOY, LOVE.` · `STILL CLOTH, BUT SOAKED THROUGH.` · `MAJEETH: THE COLOR THAT STAYS.` · then, large: `IN HIS COLOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing and give thanks. Pick something tiny you can do right here: straighten your back, take one slow, full breath, unclench your hands. Do it with attention. Then notice what made it possible: the muscles, the air, the moment of quiet. Let a thank-you rise, to whoever or whatever you understand that to be. Do it again with the next small thing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Rang, color, dye, also joy. Nothing comes by our own doing alone; in Gurbani's picture it is soaked in His rang, like cloth soaked through with dye.
Your line: in his color. Today, after you finish one piece of work, pause for a single breath and give thanks before you start the next. Day four hundred ninety-six.

497.title: Living ashtpadi 15
497.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 16, salok: no form, no color
497.howItsDone: Sikhs greet each other with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh, giving the victory to God, and the Ardas calls God the strength of the strengthless; Sukhmani's fifteenth ashtpadi lies behind both thoughts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rang, and your line: in his color. Did you pause to give thanks after finishing something? It's the end of a week that moved your weight: lean on the one, one giver, simple straight, he holds all power, he knows, in his color. Today we live the fifteenth ashtpadi. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Listen to two Sikhs meet. One says: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. The other answers: Waheguru ji ki Fateh. The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru; the victory belongs to Waheguru. It's a greeting heard at doors, on phones, at the end of speeches. But look at what it does. Every time two people meet, they hand the victory away. Whatever either of them has won, whatever they're about to win, it isn't theirs. That might sound like a recipe for feeling weak. Sikh history suggests the opposite. Today: borrowed strength.
screen: `WAHEGURU JI KA KHALSA.` → `WAHEGURU JI KI FATEH.` → `THE VICTORY IS HANDED AWAY.`

segments.voice: This week the fifteenth ashtpadi told us three things. God is brimful of every power. God knows every pain. And nothing is done on our own; it's all soaked in His color. Put those together and you might expect the result to be passivity. If all the power is God's, why bother? But in Sikh life, the result has been something like the reverse. Take the Fateh greeting. Sikh memory tells of early Khalsa Sikhs who were outnumbered, poor and hunted, and who said it anyway. In that telling, handing the victory to Waheguru didn't make them give up. It let them stand up, because their courage didn't depend on how strong they felt that morning. The Ardas, the standing prayer, has a string of names for God that make the same point. Nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, nioteaan dee ot. Honor of the dishonored, strength of the strengthless, shelter of the shelterless. Taan is strength. Nitaan is someone without it. And the One is called the strength of exactly those people. Here's the turn: strength borrowed is still strength. A tree's sap comes up from the soil, and nobody says the tree is weak. A lamp's light comes down the wire, and it still lights the room. In this tradition's picture, asking for strength rather than manufacturing it doesn't make a person less able. It makes them able in a way that doesn't run out when they do. That's why chardi kalaa, rising spirits, can survive a bad day. And it's why asking for strength isn't a sign that you've failed. In this tradition, it's the normal way strength arrives.
screen: `POWER, KNOWING, COLOR: THIS WEEK.` · `THE FATEH: VICTORY HANDED AWAY.` · `NITAANIAAN DE TAAN.` · `SAP FROM THE SOIL IS STILL SAP.` · then, large: `BORROWED STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for strength once. Think of one thing today that you don't feel strong enough for: a conversation, a task, just getting through the afternoon. Instead of bracing, try asking. If you pray, ask Waheguru plainly, in your own words, for the strength you need. If you don't pray, simply breathe in as if strength could arrive on the breath, from somewhere deeper than you. Let it come. Don't grip. The bell holds the time.
Taan, strength. The One is called the strength of the strengthless, and strength borrowed from the Giver is still strength.
Your line: borrowed strength. Today, before the hardest thing on your list, stop and ask for strength once, then go and do it. Day four hundred ninety-seven.
